# Governance, Compliance, and FinOps {#sec-governance}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One measurement: the same 100-item extraction
suite from @sec-production-eval run across a four-model ladder at temperature 0,
then evaluated as a **cascade** — answer with the cheapest model, escalate only
what a runtime validator rejects. It exists to put a number on the cost lever
everyone recommends and nobody measures. The legal dates below were read off
the current instruments in September 2026 rather than recalled, because several
of them moved in July 2026. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `llama3.2:3b`,
`qwen2.5:7b`, `qwen3.5:9b` and `gemma3:27b`; Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon.
:::

This chapter summarises law as it stood when the chapter was written, for
engineers deciding what to build. It is not legal advice, and a date or an
article number is a thing to verify against the official text rather than to
remember from here.

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- identify the lawful basis for running personal data through an LLM under
  KVKK and GDPR, and what transferring it abroad requires;
- map EU AI Act obligations onto a system you are building, with the dates as
  they now stand;
- use ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF as checklists without buying a
  certification;
- produce audit logs that answer which agent touched which data under whose
  authority;
- compute cost per session, per task and per resolved ticket, and say which
  one a budget review needs;
- measure what a small-model cascade saves, and say precisely what its
  router can and cannot see.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**This chapter states law; it is not legal advice.** Dates and obligations here
were checked in September 2026, and several of them had changed two months earlier.
Verify against the current instrument before relying on any of it, and involve
counsel for anything that matters.
:::

## KVKK and GDPR when the processor is a model {#sec-governance-kvkk}

Both regimes ask the same first question, and it is not a question about AI: on
what lawful basis are you processing this personal data? The LLM changes the
answer's difficulty in three specific ways.

**Consent is rarely the basis that fits here.** Pick the lawful basis from the
purpose and the circumstances rather than by habit. Consent is available in
principle, but it has to be freely given, specific, informed and as easy to
withdraw as to give, and a support conversation does not supply that on its own.
A customer messaging support has not thereby consented to their message being
sent to a third-party model provider, and burying it in terms of service is
exactly the pattern both regimes were written against. Most production systems
run on legitimate interest or contractual necessity instead. Contractual
necessity only covers what the contract genuinely cannot be performed without;
legitimate interest means writing down the balancing test — your interest
against the person's rights — not asserting it.

**Purpose limitation is where LLM projects fail.** Data collected to fulfil an
order and then reused to fine-tune a model is a new purpose, and a new purpose
needs its own basis. [The most common compliance failure in LLM products is not
a leak; it is training on data collected for something else.]{.hl}

**Data-subject rights have to reach the model layer.** A deletion request must
propagate to the vector store, the trace backend (@sec-observability), the eval
set (@sec-production-eval), the cache and the token mapping of
@sec-guardrails — most of which nobody thought of as a database. Reliably removing a
specific contribution from a *fine-tuned model* remains difficult and
method-dependent; the practical answer is to not put
personal data into training sets, which is a design decision made once rather
than a request handled repeatedly.

### The Turkish specifics

KVKK is Law 6698, and the part that matters most for LLM work was rewritten
recently. **Law 7499**, published 12 March 2024, amended it, and the
KVKK-amending provisions entered into force on **1 June 2024**. Two bodies
appear below: the **Authority** (Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurumu, the
institution, which receives notifications) and its decision-making **Board**
(Kurul, which issues adequacy decisions, approvals and the standard contract
texts). The rewrite brought transfer abroad — Article 9 — much closer to the
GDPR's structure:

| tier | what it is | what you must do |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Adequacy decision** | the Board has declared a country, sector or international organisation adequate | transfer on that basis |
| **Appropriate safeguards** | four of them, below | pick one, and meet its conditions |
| **Exceptional cases** | narrow derogations | do not build a product on these |

: Article 9 as amended, in the order you try them {tbl-colwidths="[24,40,36]"}

One fact turns that table into a much shorter decision. **The Board has issued
no adequacy decision for any country, sector or international organisation** —
its own page on transfers abroad says, under the heading for countries with
adequate protection, that no determination has yet been made. So the first tier
is empty in practice, and for a company using a US-hosted provider the
realistic route is the Board-published standard contract. Binding corporate
rules exist but need Board approval and a group of undertakings, which most
teams do not have. Plan for the standard contract and its five-business-day
notification; treat an adequacy decision as something that may arrive later,
not as something to look up now.

The third tier deserves one sentence, because it is where Turkish practice used
to live. Before June 2024 the usual route abroad was the data subject's
**explicit consent** (*açık rıza*). Under the amended Article 9, explicit consent
(given after being told the possible risks) is one of the exceptional cases, and
those cases are available only for **incidental** transfers — occasional,
non-recurring, outside the normal course of business. A product that sends
every conversation to a foreign provider is the opposite of incidental.

The four appropriate safeguards are: an agreement between foreign public bodies
or international organisations and Turkish public bodies (or public professional
organisations) that **does not have the status of an international treaty**,
together with Board permission —
note the negative, which is the point of the provision: a full treaty would need
parliamentary ratification, and this route deliberately allows a
lower-instrument arrangement instead; **approved binding corporate rules**
within a group of undertakings; a **Board-published standard contract**;
and a written undertaking, together with Board permission for the transfer.

#### The sectoral layer that bites first

For regulated financial institutions, Article 9 may never be reached, because a
sectoral rule cuts above it. Banks are the clearest case. The BDDK's *Regulation on Information
Systems and Electronic Banking Services* (Official Gazette 15 March 2020, in
force 1 July 2020) requires a bank's primary **and** secondary systems to be
located in Türkiye, and extends that requirement to the information systems and
backups of any outsourced provider operating within their scope. A US-hosted
model provider inside primary-system scope is therefore not a
which-safeguard question; it is not permitted. The practical routes are a
locally hosted open-weight model, a Türkiye-region deployment where the
provider offers one, or keeping the workload outside primary-system scope — and
which applies is a decision for the institution's own IT-systems compliance
function rather than for the team integrating an API. The BDDK regulation
covers banks; payment and e-money institutions answer to the Central Bank
(TCMB) and insurers to their own supervisor (SEDDK), each with its own
information-systems rules to check in the same way. Check whether a sectoral
regulator sits above KVKK for your employer *before* running the Article 9
analysis.

The operational detail engineers most often miss: **a standard contract must be
notified to the Authority within five business days of signature** (Article
9(5), and Article 14(5) of the implementing Regulation, published 10 July 2024
in Official Gazette 32598). The Authority has run an online Standard Contract
Notification Module since late 2024. [This is a calendar obligation attached to a procurement
decision, and it is missed because the person signing the contract and the
person deploying the model are not the same person.]{.hl}

Why this lands on engineers at all: choosing a US-hosted model provider *is* a
transfer abroad. It is not a platform detail; it is the Article 9 question, and
it needs answering before the integration is written rather than after.

One more Turkish artefact the LLM feature has to touch: the **personal-data
processing inventory** (*kişisel veri işleme envanteri*) — the list of which
data is processed, for what purpose, on what basis, kept how long and sent to
whom. Many controllers must also register in the Data Controllers' Registry,
**VERBİS**, which is built from that inventory. A new purpose or a new foreign
recipient — both typical of an LLM integration — means updating the inventory
and, where you are registered, the registry entry.

## What a provider contract actually promises {#sec-governance-residency}

First the two roles, because the contract is built on them. Your organisation
is the **controller** (KVKK: *veri sorumlusu*): it decides why and how the
personal data is processed, and it carries the obligations. The model provider
is normally a **processor** (*veri işleyen*): it processes the data on your
behalf and on your instructions. The contract that fixes those instructions is
usually called a **data processing agreement (DPA)**.

Vendor pages are written to reassure. The contract is the artefact, and four
things in it decide whether the deployment is lawful.

**Where the inference happens, and where it may fail over to.** A region
commitment with an unrestricted failover clause is not a region commitment.

**Whether your data trains their model, and how that is switched off.** The
default differs between a vendor's consumer tier, its API and its enterprise
agreement — for the same company. Read the tier you are actually on, and record
which one it is next to the integration.

**Retention.** "We retain inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring" is a
statement that your prompts exist somewhere for 30 days, which is a fact your
DPIA needs and which most integrations never wrote down. (A DPIA — data
protection impact assessment — is the documented risk analysis the GDPR's
Article 35 requires before high-risk processing. KVKK does not name one
explicitly, but the same analysis answers its questions too.)

**Sub-processors.** The model provider's own infrastructure suppliers are in
scope, and the list changes; the contract should oblige them to tell you when
it does.

Then the deletion question that a diagram will not answer: when a user asks to
be erased, what actually happens to the embeddings derived from their text, the
prompt caches (@sec-serving), the traces, and the golden set? Each is a copy.
Write the answer per store before you need it, because the deadline starts when
the request arrives: under the GDPR, one month (extendable by two further months
for complex requests); under KVKK, at most thirty days.

## The EU AI Act, and the dates that moved {#sec-governance-aiact}

The Act applies by risk tier, and like the GDPR it reaches beyond the EU's
borders, although its trigger is different. A Turkish company is in scope if it
places an AI system on the EU market, or if the output its system produces is
used in the EU.

The tiers, briefly. **Prohibited** practices — social scoring, certain
biometric categorisation, manipulative techniques — are out regardless of care.
**High-risk** is the tier with real engineering consequences: risk management,
data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy
and robustness, and a conformity assessment. **Limited risk** carries
transparency duties — telling people they are talking to a machine, marking
synthetic content. **Minimal risk** is everything else, which is most products.

[Most support agents are not high-risk, and the ones that are usually became so
by touching employment, credit, education or essential services.]{.hl} That
sentence is the whole classification exercise for most teams, and it is worth
doing explicitly rather than assuming either answer.

### The timeline, as it now stands

This is the part to check rather than remember, because it changed in July
2026. **Regulation (EU) 2026/1744** — the Digital Omnibus on AI — was published
in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on **27 July
2026**, deferring the high-risk obligations and changing several other
provisions:

| obligation | applies from | changed in 2026? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Prohibited practices | 2 February 2025 | no — but two added, below |
| AI literacy (Article 4) | 2 February 2025 | **content softened** — from "ensure" a sufficient level to "take measures to support" it |
| General-purpose AI (GPAI) model obligations | 2 August 2025 | no (the Commission's power to fine applies from 2 August 2026) |
| Article 50 transparency duties (all except the Article 50(2) case below) | 2 August 2026 | no |
| **Article 50(2) marking of AI-generated content, for systems placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026** | **2 December 2026** | **yes — a transitional grace period added in 2026** |
| **Two new Article 5 prohibitions** (non-consensual intimate imagery, AI-generated CSAM) | **2 December 2026** | **yes — added in 2026** |
| GPAI models placed before Aug 2025 | 2 August 2027 | no |
| **National regulatory sandboxes** | **2 August 2027** | **yes — deferred** |
| **High-risk under Annex III** (standalone) | **2 December 2027** | **yes — deferred from 2 August 2026** |
| **High-risk under Annex I** (in regulated products) | **2 August 2028** | **yes — deferred** |

: EU AI Act application dates after Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
{tbl-colwidths="[42,24,34]"}

Two things to take from the table rather than the dates themselves. The
*deferrals* applied to the high-risk tiers and to national sandboxes;
prohibitions, GPAI duties and the Article 50 date for newly placed systems all
kept their original dates, so a team that heard "the AI Act was delayed" and
stopped work heard it wrong. Note that the same regulation also **added**
obligations rather than only postponing them — two new prohibited practices from
December 2026 — gave systems already on the market a transitional period for
Article 50(2), and softened the AI-literacy duty without moving its date.
"Only high-risk changed" is the summary to avoid; read the amending articles
rather than a one-line characterisation of them, this one included. And the
December 2027 date is binding law now, not a proposal — changing it again would
need another legislative act.

A word on the GPAI rows, because they are easy to misread as yours. They bind
whoever places a **general-purpose model** on the market — the company that
trained it — not the team calling that model through an API. They matter to you
in two ways. The model's provider must give downstream integrators
documentation of its capabilities and limitations, which is exactly what your
own risk assessment needs, so ask for it. And modifying a model substantially
can make *you* its provider: the Commission's GPAI guidelines (July 2025) use,
as an indicative threshold, a modification that takes more than a third of the
original model's training compute. A typical task fine-tune is far below that.

::: {.column-margin}
The general lesson outlives the specific dates: regulatory timelines move, and
a compliance plan pinned to remembered dates is a plan that will be wrong at
some point without anyone noticing. Put the instrument's URL and the date you
checked it next to the plan, exactly as @sec-observability argues for pinning
convention versions.
:::

## Frameworks as checklists, not certifications {#sec-governance-frameworks}

Two artefacts are worth reading even if you never pursue a certificate, because
both are essentially structured lists of things teams forget.

**ISO/IEC 42001:2023** is the first international standard for an AI management
system — the ISO 27001 pattern applied to AI: policy, roles, risk assessment,
lifecycle controls, supplier management, continual improvement. It is voluntary
and certifiable, and it is increasingly asked for in enterprise procurement,
which is usually the reason it arrives on an engineering roadmap.

**The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0** (AI 100-1) organises work into
four functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — and its **Generative AI
Profile** (NIST AI 600-1, released 26 July 2024) is the more directly useful
document: twelve risk categories specific to or amplified by generative AI, with
over two hundred suggested actions.

The honest way to use them: [read the risk categories as a list of things to
have an answer for, and notice which ones your team has never discussed.]{.hl}
That exercise takes an afternoon and finds real gaps. Pursuing certification is
a separate, much larger decision, driven by whether customers require it.

## Audit logging: who did what, to whose data, under whose authority {#sec-governance-audit}

@sec-observability's tracing answers *what happened technically*. An audit log
answers a different question — *who authorised this* — and the two have
different retention, different access controls and different readers.

The fields an auditor asks for, none of which can be added retrospectively:

```text
  when            timestamp, and the time zone it is in
  who             the human principal, not just the service account
  on behalf of    the user whose data was processed
  what            the action, and the tool that performed it
  which data      identifiers or categories touched — not the content
  authority       the lawful basis, or the approval that permitted it
  where           region of processing, and the model provider
  outcome         succeeded, failed, refused, escalated
```

Three properties separate an audit log from an application log. **It is
append-only**, because a log an operator can edit answers nothing. **It records
the authority, not just the action** — "issued a refund" is an event; "issued a
refund under approval #4821 by user X" is an audit record. And **it is
retained on its own schedule**, usually longer than traces and shorter than the
business record, which means it is a separate store with a separate policy.

For agents specifically, one addition: log the **decision to act** as well as
the act. When an agent chose a tool, what did it have in context? That is the
question every incident review asks, and @sec-agent-security is why it matters
— the answer is how you find out whether the instruction came from your user or
from a document.

## Unit economics: which number a budget review needs {#sec-governance-unit}

Cost per request is the number you have and the wrong one to report. Three
levels, and only the last survives contact with a budget-holder:

| metric | what it flatters | when it is right |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **cost per request** | verbose systems that answer in many steps | capacity planning |
| **cost per session** | a feature nobody completes | comparing feature usage |
| **cost per resolved task** | nothing — it is the honest one | any budget conversation |

: Three unit costs {tbl-colwidths="[26,40,34]"}

Computing the third honestly means including what teams routinely leave out:
retried calls, the runs that hit a ceiling (@sec-deployment), the judge calls in
online evaluation (@sec-production-eval), the embedding calls, and **the cost of
the human who handled the escalation**. That last one is usually the largest
single term and the one omitted, because it sits in a different budget.

[The comparison that matters is against the human-only baseline, on the same
definition of resolved.]{.hl} An agent that resolves 60% of tickets at €0.08
each and escalates the rest to a human at €4.00 costs
$0.08 + 0.40 \times 4.00 = $ **€1.68** per ticket against a human-only baseline
of €4.00 — a 58% reduction. Note that the agent is paid on the escalated
tickets too: you only learn it failed by running it, and quietly dropping that
term is exactly the omission the paragraph above warns about. Note also the
second assumption, which the arithmetic cannot see: an escalated ticket is
priced the same as a fresh one, and escalations are by construction the hard
ones. Re-run it with escalations at €6.00: the cost becomes €2.48 per ticket,
and the 58% reduction shrinks to 38%. That arithmetic is the business case, and it is
sensitive almost entirely to the resolution rate rather than to the token price
— which is why @sec-production-eval's measurement discipline is a cost
discipline too.

## What a cascade actually saves {#sec-governance-cascade}

"Route the easy requests to a smaller model" is the most-recommended cost lever
in this field and the least-measured. So here it is measured, on
@sec-production-eval's 100-item Turkish extraction suite, at temperature 0, with
four local models.

First the ladder alone. Each item has five fields, so *field acc* is the share
of the 500 individual field decisions that were right, and *exact* counts the
items with all five fields right:

```text
100 items, 500 field decisions, temperature 0

model            field acc   exact   passes validator   output tokens
llama3.2:3b         92.40%      65             80/100            4,205
qwen2.5:7b          95.20%      80             96/100            5,105
qwen3.5:9b          97.80%      90            100/100            6,173
gemma3:27b         100.00%     100            100/100            4,921
```

Two things before the cascade. `gemma3:27b` got **every field of every item
right** — a perfect 100/100 exact match, which is worth noting because it means
100% is actually reachable on this suite, not a limit the models only approach. And note that the biggest model
used *fewer* output tokens than the 9B one: verbosity is not a function of size,
so a token-based cost estimate cannot be derived from parameter count.

### The cascade: answer cheap, escalate on a validator

The router is not a difficulty predictor. It is the schema-and-format check of
@sec-decoding, run on the small model's output: does it parse, does it have all
five fields, does the order code match its pattern, is the month a real month,
is the amount formatted like an amount. **It uses no ground truth** — it is
exactly what you could run in production.

```text
small -> big              escalated   field acc   exact
llama3.2:3b -> qwen2.5:7b       20%      96.20%      81
llama3.2:3b -> qwen3.5:9b       20%      96.20%      82
llama3.2:3b -> gemma3:27b       20%      97.00%      85
qwen2.5:7b  -> qwen3.5:9b        4%      96.20%      82
qwen2.5:7b  -> gemma3:27b        4%      96.60%      84
qwen3.5:9b  -> gemma3:27b         0%      97.80%      90
```

The headline is the third row. [Sending **20%** of requests to the large model
recovers most of the quality gap: 92.40% alone, 97.00% cascaded, 100.00% if
everything went to the large model.]{.hl} That is 61% of the gap closed for one
request in five.

The economics follow from the escalation rate and need no invented prices. You
pay the small model on everything and the large model on the escalated share, so
if the large model costs *K* times the small one per request, the cascade costs
$(1 + 0.20K)/K$ of large-model-only:

```text
  K = 10   ->  30% of the large-model bill
  K = 30   ->  23%
```

*K* is a ratio of cost per request, not of list price per token. The two differ
whenever the models are not equally verbose, and the token column above shows
that they are not.

The 7B→27B row is the same lever at a different setting: **4% escalation** for
96.60%, a 1.4-point gain over the 7B alone. What that costs depends on the price
ratio and not on the escalation rate alone — at $K = 10$ the cascade is
$(1 + 0.04 \times 10)/10 = 14\%$ of large-model-only but $1.4\times$ the 7B's
own bill. "Almost no additional spend" is true relative to the large model and
false relative to the small one; say which baseline you mean.

### The row that teaches the most is the last one

`qwen3.5:9b -> gemma3:27b` escalates **0%** of requests, so the cascade is just
the 9B model and buys exactly nothing. That is not a failure of the idea; it is
the idea's boundary, stated precisely.

The 9B model passes the validator on **100 of 100** items while being correct on
only **97.80%** of fields. [The validator checks well-formedness, and
well-formedness stops correlating with correctness as soon as the model is good
enough to always be well-formed.]{.hl} A perfectly formatted JSON object with
the wrong city in it is invisible to every check that does not know the right
answer.

Three consequences worth carrying:

**Measure the escalation rate, not the predicted difficulty.**
@sec-classification measured an LLM's *verbalised* confidence as a detector of
its own errors at **AUROC 0.667** — real signal, not enough to route on. (AUROC
here is the probability that a randomly chosen wrong answer gets a lower
confidence than a randomly chosen right one; 0.5 is chance.) On the
same task a fine-tuned classifier's own probability reached **0.843**, which is
the honest shape of the trade: a model asked how sure it is answers worse —
partly because its stated numbers are coarse, nearly always the same value — and
a model's own output distribution answers considerably better. A validator is different again —
a fact about the output you already have rather than a prediction about a
request you have not run.

**The cascade's ceiling is what your router can see.** If your only signal is
schema validity, you can only escalate malformedness. Adding a signal the
router *can* see — a confidence score, a retrieval-grounding check, a
disagreement between two cheap models — is what raises the ceiling, and each
costs something.

**Do not report the saving without the quality column.** 3B→27B is a 3.0-point
drop in field accuracy and a **15-point** drop in exact match against
large-model-only. Whether that is acceptable is a product decision, and it can
only be made if both numbers are on the table.

::: {.column-margin}
Wall-clock timings were recorded but are not reported as costs: this ran on a
shared laptop where the same work varied by an order of magnitude between runs.
The escalation rate and token counts are the load-bearing numbers, and they are
the ones that transfer to your prices.
:::

### The other levers, in the order to try them

@sec-serving established the ordering and this chapter's measurement completes
it. Prompt caching and removing genuinely redundant tokens first, because they
carry no quality risk: caching serves the same input more cheaply, and
@sec-serving measured warm prefill flat at 12–16 ms and a 9.0× whole-request
improvement at 4,247 tokens. Cutting context the model actually uses is a
different lever — it can lower quality, so it belongs in the eval. Then batch
APIs where latency is not user-facing. Then the cascade, which does carry quality risk and now has a number attached.
Then distillation and quantisation, which are projects rather than settings.

## Making the safe path the fast path {#sec-governance-org}

Governance that depends on a review queue fails at the same point every time:
when a team has a deadline. The alternative is to put the controls in the
default path.

**An agent registry**, which @sec-capstone builds out in full: one row per agent listing its
tools, its data access, its owner, its lawful basis and its reversibility
profile. It is the artefact every audit, incident and cost review needs, and it
cannot be reconstructed after the fact.

**A golden path**, meaning a template repository where the eval gate
(@sec-production-eval), tracing with cost dimensions (@sec-observability), the
PII boundary (@sec-guardrails) and tool classification are already wired. The
measure of success is that the compliant way is the fastest way to ship.

**Cost attribution from the first agent**, because @sec-observability's
dimensions cannot be added retrospectively, and because the unit economics above
are impossible without them. Pair it with **token budgets** per team or per key,
enforced at the gateway (@sec-gateway), so that a runaway agent loop becomes an
alert rather than an invoice.

**A model registry with pinned versions** (@sec-gateway), with the provider's
model card or documentation stored next to each version. It is simultaneously a
cost control, a quality control and a compliance artefact: the AI Act's logging
and documentation duties for high-risk systems require you to trace which system
version produced an output.

## Intuition checks {#sec-governance-intuition}

Answer each before opening it. The first three are legal facts that changed or
are commonly misremembered; the last three carry the measurement.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. "The EU AI Act was delayed, so we have more time." Is that right?

Only partly. The delay applies mainly to the high-risk tiers, and reading it
as a general delay is a common and expensive mistake.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — the Digital Omnibus, in force 27 July 2026 —
deferred Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026 to **2 December
2027**, and Annex I ones to **2 August 2028**. Most other dates held:
prohibited practices and AI literacy since 2 February 2025 (the literacy duty
itself was softened), GPAI obligations since 2 August 2025, Article 50
transparency duties from 2 August 2026. The amendment also carries specific
transitional exceptions, including a grace period to 2 December 2026 under
Article 50(2) for certain systems already on the market. The timeline above
lists them.

So if your obligation is transparency — telling people they are talking to a
machine, marking synthetic content — most of it was not delayed, and the
exceptions are narrow enough to check against the timeline rather than
assume. And the December 2027 date is binding law now, not a proposal.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. You pick a US-hosted model provider. Whose problem is that?

Yours, at design time. Choosing that provider *is* a transfer of personal data
abroad under KVKK Article 9, not a platform detail to sort out later.

The amended Article 9 — rewritten by Law 7499, in force 1 June 2024 — gives a
tiered structure: an adequacy decision, or one of four appropriate safeguards
(an agreement between public bodies that does not have the status of an
international treaty, with Board permission; approved binding corporate
rules; a Board-published standard contract; or a written undertaking, with
Board permission), or a narrow derogation you should not build a product on. The
derogations, explicit consent among them, cover only incidental, non-recurring
transfers.

The detail that gets missed: a standard contract must be **notified to the
Authority within five business days of signature**. That is a calendar
obligation attached to a procurement decision, and it is missed because the
person signing and the person integrating are different people.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A user asks to be deleted. What actually has to happen?

Far more than deleting the row, and the list is the reason to design for it
rather than handle it.

Their data is also in the vector store, the trace backend
(@sec-observability), the eval set (@sec-production-eval), the prompt cache (@sec-serving)
and the token mapping of @sec-guardrails — none of which anyone
thinks of as a database.

And if it reached a fine-tuned model, reliable removal of that contribution
remains difficult and method-dependent — whether
model weights *contain* personal data at all is contested and fact-dependent,
which is precisely why you do not want the question to be live for your product.
The practical answer is not a better deletion pipeline; it is not putting
personal data into training sets, which is one design decision instead of a
recurring request. Two further boundaries worth knowing: the right to erasure
has exceptions — a legal retention obligation, or the establishment and defence
of legal claims — and genuinely *anonymised* data falls outside the regime
entirely, while *pseudonymised* data (linkable to a person only with extra
information kept separately) does not. Anonymisation that survives scrutiny is
harder than removing the obvious identifiers. Write down what happens per store
before the first request arrives, because the deadline — one month under the
GDPR, thirty days under KVKK — starts when it does.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. How much does routing easy requests to a small model actually save?

Measured on a 100-item extraction suite with four local models: sending **20%**
of requests to the large model took field accuracy from **92.40%** (3B alone) to
**97.00%**, against **100.00%** for the large model on everything — 61% of the
gap for one request in five.

The economics need no invented prices, but they do need *yours*. You pay the
small model on everything and the large one on the escalated share, so at a cost
ratio *K* the cascade costs $(1 + 0.20K)/K$ of large-model-only: **30%** of the
bill at K = 10, **23%** at K = 30. Those are scenarios computed from an assumed
ratio, not a measured provider invoice — the accuracy column is measured, the
percentages are arithmetic. Substitute your own $K$, and remember it differs for
input and output tokens.

Report the quality column too: that cascade is 3.0 points of field accuracy and
**15 points of exact match** below large-model-only. A saving quoted without it
is not a result.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Should the router predict which requests are hard?

Prefer a validator over a predictor.

@sec-classification measured a model's verbalised confidence as a detector of
its own errors at **AUROC 0.667**, against 0.843 for a fine-tuned classifier's
own probability on the same task — real signal, not enough to route on
blindly. The cascade here instead runs the cheap model and
checks its output: does it parse, are all fields present, does each match its
expected format. That is a fact about an output you already have rather than a
guess about a request you have not run, and it uses no ground truth, so it runs
in production unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your cascade escalates 0% of requests. Great news?

No — it means the cascade is doing nothing, and it shows you the limit of the
whole technique.

Measured: `qwen3.5:9b` passed the format validator on **100 of 100** items while
being correct on only **97.80%** of fields. So nothing escalated, the cascade
collapsed to the 9B model, and it saved nothing over just using that model.

The lesson generalises. A validator checks well-formedness, and well-formedness
stops correlating with correctness as soon as the model is reliably
well-formed — a perfectly formatted JSON object with the wrong city in it is
invisible to any check that does not know the answer. Raising the ceiling means
adding a signal the router *can* see: a confidence score, a grounding check, or
disagreement between two cheap models. Each costs something.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-governance-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurement makes answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the obligations

**Q: What is the lawful basis for sending customer messages to an LLM
provider?**

Start by saying it is not usually consent — a customer contacting support has
not consented to third-party processing, and burying it in terms of service is
the pattern the regimes were written against. Most systems run on legitimate
interest or contractual necessity; for legitimate interest that means
documenting the balancing test. Then name the two traps: purpose limitation, because reusing order data to
fine-tune is a new purpose needing its own basis; and transfer abroad, because
choosing a US-hosted provider is the Article 9 question and needs answering
before the integration is written.

**Q: Is your system high-risk under the EU AI Act?**

Most support agents are not; the ones that are usually became so by touching
employment, credit, education or essential services. Then show you know the
timeline as it now stands rather than as it was drafted: Regulation (EU)
2026/1744 deferred Annex III high-risk to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to
2 August 2028, while prohibitions, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency for
newly placed systems kept their original dates, and it added two new
prohibitions from December 2026. Saying "the Act was delayed" without that
distinction is the wrong answer.

**Q: What goes in an audit log that is not in a trace?**

The authority. A trace says a refund was issued; an audit record says it was
issued on behalf of this user, under this approval, by this principal, in this
region, under this lawful basis. It is append-only, it has its own retention
schedule, and for agents it should record the decision to act as well as the
act — what was in context when the agent chose a tool is the question every
incident review asks (@sec-agent-security).

### Testing whether you have run one

**Q: Your CFO asks what the AI feature costs. What do you report?**

Cost per resolved task, not per request or per session — the first flatters
verbose systems and the second flatters features nobody completes. Include what
teams leave out: retries, ceiling hits, online judge calls, embeddings, and the
cost of the human handling escalations, which is usually the largest term and
sits in someone else's budget. Then give the comparison that makes it a business
case: the human-only baseline on the same definition of resolved. The arithmetic
is far more sensitive to resolution rate than to token price.

**Q: How would you cut inference cost by half without losing quality?**

In order of quality risk. Prompt caching and removing genuinely redundant tokens
first, because they carry none — caching serves the same input, measured in
@sec-serving as warm prefill flat at 12–16 ms and 9.0× on the whole request at
4,247 tokens. Cutting context the model uses is not free: it is a quality
decision for the eval. Then batch APIs where latency is not
user-facing. Then a cascade, with a number: escalating 20% of requests recovered
61% of the quality gap here, costing 30% of the large-model bill at a 10×
price ratio. Then quantisation and distillation, which are projects.

**Q: Your cascade's router is a schema validator. What are you blind to?**

Everything that is well-formed and wrong. Measured here, the 9B model passed the
validator on 100 of 100 items while being correct on 97.8% of fields, so the
cascade escalated nothing and saved nothing. The general statement is that a
validator's ceiling is what it can see, and well-formedness decouples from
correctness as models improve. To go further you need a signal about
correctness — confidence, grounding, or disagreement between two cheap models —
and each of those costs something you should measure before adopting.

## Lab: the compliance and cost pass {#sec-governance-lab}

### Step 1 — write the data flow, including the copies

One page: what personal data enters, which stores hold it, which leave your
region, and how long each keeps it. Include the trace backend, the eval set, the
cache and the token mapping. The copies people forget are the finding.

### Step 2 — answer the transfer question

For each provider, name the Article 9 basis you are relying on. If it is a
standard contract, find out whether it was notified to the Authority within five
business days — and if nobody knows, that is the deliverable.

### Step 3 — classify your system under the AI Act

Prohibited, high-risk, limited or minimal, with the reasoning written down.
Then check the current dates against the instrument rather than against this
chapter, and record the date you checked.

### Step 4 — walk a deletion request through every store

Pick a real user id and trace what would have to happen in each store from step
1. Time it. Anything you cannot answer is a design task, not a process gap.

### Step 5 — compute cost per resolved task

Include retries, ceiling hits, judge calls, embeddings and the human escalation
cost. Compare against the human-only baseline on the same definition of
resolved. Then compute how sensitive the result is to the resolution rate.

### Step 6 — measure your own cascade

Run your suite on two models, build a runtime validator that uses no ground
truth, and measure the escalation rate and the resulting quality. Report the
saving as a function of your price ratio, and report the quality drop next to
it.

### Step 7 — find your validator's blind spot

Take the items your validator accepted and count how many were actually wrong.
That number is the ceiling on what a cascade can do for you, and it is the one
that decides whether to invest in a better signal.

### What to hand in

The data-flow page with every copy listed; the Article 9 basis per provider and
its notification status; your AI Act classification with the date you checked
the dates; the deletion walk-through with its gaps; cost per resolved task
against the human baseline; and your cascade's escalation rate, quality drop and
validator blind-spot count.

## Exercises {#sec-governance-exercises}

1. **The copies inventory.** List every store in your system that holds a copy
   of user text. Rank them by whether a deletion request currently reaches them.

2. **Read one contract.** Take your model provider's actual terms — the tier you
   are on, not the marketing page — and extract four facts: processing region
   and failover, training on your data, retention period, sub-processor
   notification. Note which you could not find.

3. **Classify honestly.** Write your AI Act classification and then argue the
   opposite case in a paragraph. If the opposite case is easy to argue, get
   advice.

4. **Cost per resolved task.** Compute it including the human escalation cost,
   then recompute at resolution rates 10 points higher and lower. Report which
   input the business case is most sensitive to.

5. **Your escalation rate.** Build a schema validator for your own output and
   measure what fraction of a small model's responses it rejects. Convert that
   to a saving at your own price ratio.

6. **The blind spot.** Of the outputs your validator accepted, hand-check fifty
   for correctness. Report the rate, and say whether a better router is worth
   building.

7. **Date drift.** Take three regulatory dates your compliance plan depends on
   and verify each against the current instrument. Record the URL and the date
   you checked, then set a reminder to do it again.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-governance-deeper}

Before reading: write down, from memory, which lawful basis your product relies
on and where its data is processed. Then check. The gap between those two is
this chapter's subject.

This chapter cites no papers, so there is one table. Most sources below are a
primary instrument or its official guidance, because on this material secondary
summaries go stale silently — as the July 2026 amendment demonstrates. The
timeline tracker in the first row is a well-maintained secondary source and
worth having; check it against the Official Journal text before you rely on a
date.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [EU AI Act implementation timeline](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation-timeline/) | a secondary tracker, kept current, including the 2026 changes; convenient, and not the authority |
| [Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 on EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng) | the Digital Omnibus on AI itself — the amending articles, in force, and the only place the transitional provisions are stated exactly |
| [KVKK — transfer abroad](https://www.kvkk.gov.tr/Icerik/2053/Yurtdisina-Aktarim) | the Authority's own page on amended Article 9, with the standard contracts and the notification module |
| [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) | AI RMF 1.0 and the Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1); the twelve risk categories are the most useful checklist in this chapter |
| ISO/IEC 42001:2023 | the AI management system standard; voluntary and certifiable, and increasingly asked for in enterprise procurement |
| [FinOps Framework](https://www.finops.org/framework/) | the cost-management vocabulary this chapter borrows — inform, optimise, operate — applied to a new kind of variable cost |
| [`litellm`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) | per-key budgets and spend attribution; the practical route from @sec-gateway's choke point to unit economics |

: Beyond this chapter {tbl-colwidths="[34,66]"}

## What to remember {#sec-governance-summary}

- **The lawful basis is rarely consent, and purpose limitation is where LLM
  projects fail.** Data collected to fulfil an order and reused to fine-tune is
  a new purpose needing its own basis. [The most common compliance failure in
  LLM products is not a leak; it is training on data collected for something
  else.]{.hl}

- **Choosing a model provider is a transfer decision, made at design time.**
  KVKK Article 9, as rewritten by Law 7499 (in force 1 June 2024), gives
  adequacy, then four appropriate safeguards, then narrow derogations. A
  standard contract must be **notified to the Authority within five business
  days of signature** — a calendar obligation attached to a procurement
  decision.

- **The AI Act's high-risk dates moved, and they were not the only change.**
  Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026, deferred Annex III to
  **2 December 2027**, Annex I to **2 August 2028** and national sandboxes to
  August 2027. It also added two prohibitions that apply from 2 December 2026,
  gave systems already on the market until that date for Article 50(2), and
  softened the AI-literacy duty.
  Prohibitions (Feb 2025), GPAI duties (Aug 2025) and Article 50 transparency
  for newly placed systems (Aug 2026) kept their dates. "The Act was delayed" is
  wrong for most teams' actual obligations.

- **Deletion reaches more stores than anyone lists.** Vector store, traces, eval
  set, prompt cache, token mapping — and a fine-tuned model, where reliable
  erasure remains difficult and method-dependent. Design for it once instead of handling it repeatedly.

- **An audit log records authority, not just action**, is append-only, keeps its
  own retention schedule, and for agents should capture the decision to act as
  well as the act.

- **Report cost per resolved task**, including retries, ceiling hits, judge
  calls and the human escalation cost — usually the largest term and in someone
  else's budget. The business case is far more sensitive to resolution rate than
  to token price.

- **A cascade is a real lever with a measured size.** Escalating **20%** of
  requests to the large model took field accuracy from **92.40%** to **97.00%**
  against **100.00%** for large-model-only — 61% of the gap for one request in
  five, costing $(1+0.2K)/K$ of the large-model bill, or **30%** at a 10× price
  ratio. Report the quality drop with it: 3.0 points of field accuracy and
  **15 points of exact match**.

- **Route on a validator, not on predicted difficulty.** @sec-classification
  measured verbalised confidence at AUROC 0.667 as a detector of a model's own
  errors, against 0.843 for a real probability; a schema-and-format check is a fact
  about an output you already have, uses no ground truth, and runs unchanged in
  production.

- **A validator's ceiling is what it can see.** The 9B model passed the format
  check on **100 of 100** items while being correct on **97.80%** of fields, so
  its cascade escalated **0%** and saved nothing. [Well-formedness stops
  correlating with correctness as soon as the model is reliably
  well-formed]{.hl} — going further needs a signal about correctness, and each
  one costs something.
